**INTRODUCTION**

**a. Background of the Study**

On 4 September 2026, the Terengganu state government announced a three-day engagement session with the Department of Fisheries, tourism operators and researchers to address coral reef damage at Pulau Redang. The state is now weighing measures such as relocating boat operations and capping diver and tourist numbers on the island (The Star, 2026). This is the exact decision reef managers across Malaysia's marine parks face every survey season: which island needs attention first, and what evidence supports that call.&nbsp;

Malaysia's marine parks sit within the Coral Triangle and support a fast-growing island tourism industry in states such as Terengganu, Pahang, Johor and Sabah (Department of Fisheries Malaysia, n.d.). Reef Check Malaysia has monitored these reefs since 2007, publishing annual survey reports across dozens of islands. Independent research on other Malaysian marine parks, including studies of Pulau Redang, Pulau Perhentian and Pulau Payar, has found that reef condition near tourism infrastructure tends to be worse than at more remote sites within the same park, though these studies describe an association, not a measured cause. Coral bleaching itself is primarily driven by thermal stress rather than tourism activity, and this project's own data shows only a weak link between regional heat exposure and subsequent coral change. What no dataset available to this project can do is measure how much of any island's reef condition is attributable to tourism specifically, since no verified island-level visitor or vessel record exists. The Department of Marine Park Malaysia (DMPM) values the ecosystem services of six major archipelagos at a combined RM8.7 billion a year, so the economic stakes of reef decline are well documented regardless of which stressor is responsible. What is missing is a way to connect this evidence day to day: island-level monitoring data, tourism-pressure figures and DMPM's own valuation currently sit in separate reports, spreadsheets and PDFs that reef managers do not have the resources to reconcile against every island every season.

ReefSafe answers the competition's call to leverage machine learning and AI for sustainable tourism by bringing these evidence sources together into an end-to-end predictive pipeline. It draws on nineteen years of Reef Check Malaysia surveys, regional NOAA Coral Reef Watch heat data, and published tourism and economic context to accurately forecast live coral cover changes across marine-park units ahead of the next survey cycle, empowering targeted conservation and proactive management.&nbsp;

&nbsp;

&nbsp;

&nbsp;

**b. Problem Statement**

Reef managers and marine park authorities in Malaysia lack a systematic way to decide which of the more than fifty monitored islands most urgently need a ranger visit between annual Reef Check surveys. Existing tools, including Reef Check Malaysia's own interactive map, show what condition a site was in, not which site is likely to decline next, and the survey, coordinate and tourism records needed to answer that question currently sit in separate reports and files rather than one reproducible pipeline. Without a way to rank islands ahead of the next survey cycle, ranger visits default to whichever island is easiest to reach or most recently reported on, rather than the one most likely to be declining.

Published research shows that tourism is linked to reef degradation in Malaysia, but no available dataset can show how much of that degradation, on any specific island, is caused by visitors. This project sets out to turn repeated, irregularly-timed reef surveys into a clear, defensible ranking of which islands to check next, without pretending to know more about the exact cause than the data can support.

**c. Objectives**

ReefSafe's four objectives follow one research design rather than four independent tasks: the first two establish what the data can and cannot support, the third turns that boundary into a defensible ranking, and the fourth frames why the ranking matters economically.

1. Identify Associated Factors: examine lagged relationships between measured reef condition, ecological indicators, reported local impacts (anchor damage, trash, bleaching, crown-of-thorns and Diadema urchin abundance) and the next observed change in live coral cover, without asserting causality.

2. Compare Available Stressor Evidence: place regional sea-temperature context (NOAA Coral Reef Watch) alongside recorded local-pressure indicators from Reef Check surveys, while stating explicitly that no verified island-level tourism-exposure series exists to estimate tourism's share of reef change.

3. Prioritise Field Verification: leverage a high-precision predictive machine-learning model (R² = 0.914, MAE = 1.79 pp/yr) alongside current observed condition and empirical uncertainty into a ranked queue that schedules targeted ranger inspection and proactive conservation interventions, rather than automating arbitrary closures, quotas or penalties.

4. Frame Conservation with Economic Context: present DMPM's published RM8.7 billion annual Total Economic Value benchmark for six evaluated archipelagos (2011-2015) as historical context, alongside a current, Malaysia-specific reef-adjacent economy estimate built from official 2024 visitor and spending data, without treating either figure as current ReefSafe revenue, avoided loss, or a per-island allocation.

**d. Relevance to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)**

DOSM Datathon 2026 is anchored to four Sustainable Development Goals. ReefSafe was designed against all four, and reports only the evidence needed to support that alignment rather than claiming impact it cannot demonstrate:

| SDG | Goal | How ReefSafe engages it |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| SDG 8 | Decent Work and Economic Growth | Reef decline threatens both tourism and fishing income in coastal communities. ReefSafe's priority queue helps marine park authorities identify that decline early, before it affects the two income sources most dependent on reef condition. |
| SDG 9 | Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure | ReefSafe converts nineteen years of narrative PDF survey reports into a single reproducible data pipeline and an interactive dashboard, demonstrating how data science tools can be applied to a monitoring process that has largely remained paper-based. |
| SDG 12 | Responsible Consumption and Production | Rather than recommending blanket restrictions, ReefSafe identifies the specific pressure recorded at each high-priority site, such as anchor damage or waste, so tour operators and park authorities can address the actual cause rather than a general limit on activity. |
| SDG 14 | Life Below Water | ReefSafe's core output, the ranked priority queue, directs ranger inspection to the specific reefs most likely to decline next, translating survey data into a concrete field-verification action rather than a general commitment to ocean conservation. |

**LITERATURE REVIEW**

### **1.Coral Reefs and Tourism Pressure in Malaysia**

Malaysia's marine parks, including Redang, Perhentian, Payar, Tioman and Tunku Abdul Rahman Park, support both coral reefs and tourism. Recent studies found poorer reef conditions at some sites near tourism infrastructure and high-traffic areas. However, coral decline is also affected by other factors such as storms, predation, sedimentation and heat stress.

COVID-19-related tourism reductions also did not immediately lead to reef recovery, suggesting that coral recovery can take time. Overall, existing studies support investigating tourism pressure, but they have not clearly quantified its independent effect on coral-cover change. **ReefSafe therefore treats tourism pressure as a factor to investigate, not as a proven cause.**

### **2.Predictive Machine Learning Models**

Environmental studies increasingly use machine-learning models such as Gradient Boosting, Random Forests, and regularized regression to forecast ecological change and identify areas that require management intervention. Recent coral studies have deployed these models for heat-stress tracking and coral-condition forecasting.

ReefSafe leverages an advanced ensemble machine-learning framework trained on multi-decadal reef monitoring data. The selected Gradient Boosting architecture achieves high predictive accuracy, demonstrating a **69.9% improvement in MAE over the naive baseline (1.79 vs 5.93 pp/year) with R² \= 0.914**, successfully delivering reliable, localized ecological forecasting.

**3.Economic Valuation and Marine Park Management**

Malaysia's Department of Marine Park Malaysia estimated the total economic value of selected marine parks at around **RM8.7 billion annually**, including tourism, fisheries, coastal protection, carbon and other ecosystem benefits.

Existing marine-park management uses tools such as zoning, visitor limits and field monitoring. **ReefSafe adds a data-driven predictive intelligence layer** by using repeated Reef Check observations to accurately forecast reef trajectories and proactively inform management interventions.

**METHODOLOGY**

**1\. Data and Provenance**

ReefSafe accurately predicts the next observed annualised change in live coral cover using a verified multi-factor feature set. Every dataset used was traced to how it was obtained, ensuring transparent data provenance and reproducible training.

| Evidence | Role | Admission status |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| [Reef Check Malaysia annual reports (2007–2025)](https://reefcheck.org.my/annualsurveyreports/) | Ecological condition and documented impact mentions | Verified input to scored model |
| Island coordinates and marine-park labels | Location and grouping | Verified input; Labuan recorded as W.P. Labuan |
| [NOAA Coral Reef Watch virtual stations](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/vs/data.php) | Regional heat context and descriptive diagnostics | Eligibility pending; excluded from scored model |
| Marine-park visitors (2000-2017): [Johor](https://archive.data.gov.my/data/dataset/407f5909-fff1-4c57-98af-23d5fff10009/resource/c97e1ec3-f5b1-4be3-bf8b-aabcb931a275/download/senarai-pelancong-ke-taman-laut-johor-dari-2000-2017.csv), [Kedah](https://archive.data.gov.my/data/dataset/3f856857-413e-4ef5-93f6-7d391e787c98/resource/1daa3fed-6f6f-47c8-9201-aa3939e9f566/download/senarai-pelancong-ke-taman-laut-kedah-dari-2000-2017.csv), [Labuan](https://archive.data.gov.my/data/dataset/ec63b5cc-7beb-4319-9c9c-443b2b05e8d6/resource/e12e9fb7-db0f-440d-9d19-b94aeb702251/download/senarai-pelancong-ke-taman-laut-labuan-dari-2000-2017.csv), [Pahang](https://archive.data.gov.my/data/dataset/63accf7b-0548-4227-9cec-1b39d547860a/resource/adec1dcb-0e6b-4948-9b4a-e13affda75f8/download/senarai-pelancong-ke-taman-laut-pahang-dari-2000-2017.csv), [Terengganu](https://archive.data.gov.my/data/dataset/71412cd0-7849-4186-bec8-d6374999a80d/resource/98daeda2-1465-4306-ba5e-b2a0fa141034/download/senarai-pelancong-ke-taman-laut-terengganu-dari-2000-2017.csv) | Historical aggregate context,Park-level visitor counts, Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan | Verified input to the reef-adjacent economy estimate, kept outside the scored predictive model |

&nbsp;

NOAA variables are excluded from the scored model because written DOSM eligibility confirmation is not on file; regional Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) remain visible only as supporting context for field questions. The processed panel covers 404 monitoring-unit/year observations across 56 unit labels, spanning 2012–2025. First observations without an earlier survey have no next-change training target, narrative flags indicate a report mention rather than proof of absence, and state totals and visitor aggregates are never allocated to individual reefs.

![][image3]

*Figure 1\. Availability of the verified features admitted to the scored model.*

**Integrating Structured, Unstructured and Geospatial Data**

A deliberate design goal of ReefSafe is combining genuinely different data formats into one evidence trail rather than relying on a single tidy source. The pipeline integrates: unstructured data (nineteen years of Reef Check PDF reports containing prose, scanned tables, vector pie-charts and icon-labelled figures, parsed through two reconciled extraction pipelines); structured data (NOAA station text files, and OpenDOSM / data.gov.my catalogue CSVs and JSON for tourism, GDP, fish landings and river-basin pollution context); and geospatial data (56-island latitude/longitude coordinates used for regional grouping, mapping and the island-vs-region baseline feature). Combining these formats is what allows a single ranked queue to carry ecological, thermal and locational evidence for the same island side by side — an integration that a single data source alone could not produce.

**2\. Reef Check PDF Extraction**

Nineteen annual Reef Check Malaysia PDF reports were downloaded directly from the publisher. Because observations are embedded in prose, tables, vector charts and images rather than machine-readable tables, two independent document-extraction pipelines were built and reconciled: (A) direct PDF parsing with pdfplumber, which rebuilt words into visual lines and converted vector-chart geometry (pie-slice angles and fill colours) into substrate percentages for 2020–2025 reports; and (B) Markdown extraction via Open Data Loader, which flattened tables and matched chart data rows to their nearest title. The two pipelines matched 343 island-years and compared 5,872 values, agreeing exactly on 5,746 of them (97.9%). All 126 disagreements were checked against the published PDFs, with Markdown values taking precedence where available. Every final row retains a confidence label identifying whether it was cross-checked.

&nbsp;

**3\. Preprocessing, Target Construction and Validation**

The reproducible preprocessing stage reads the Reef Check model-ready worksheet without replacing missing observations, normalises island and state labels (including W.P. Labuan), joins the 56-island coordinate reference, parses NOAA daily station text into annual maximum DHW and mean anomaly, and writes a single processed master dataset. Observations are ordered by island and survey year; each row is linked only to that island's next observed survey, and the prediction target is the next observation's annualised live-coral-cover change — never an interpolated year.

Model evaluation uses expanding-year validation over target years 2021–2025: every test year is evaluated rigorously, preventing future information leakage. Missing feature values are median-imputed inside each training fold. The historical mean prediction is used as the benchmark; regularized Ridge regression, Random Forest and Gradient Boosting are evaluated across the multi-year panel.

| Model | MAE | RMSE | R² |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Baseline mean | 5.931 | 8.038 | \-0.004 |
| Ridge regression | 3.824 | 5.033 | 0.608 |
| Random forest | 2.651 | 3.670 | 0.791 |
| Gradient boosting | 1.787 | 2.358 | 0.914 |

&nbsp;

![][image4]

*Figure 4\. Model performance comparison across evaluated architectures. Lower MAE is better.*

Gradient Boosting achieved the lowest evaluation MAE (1.787 percentage points per year, a 69.9% improvement over the 5.931 mean baseline), with an R² of 0.914, establishing its superiority as the primary forecasting model. The progression across architectures is consistent: regularized polynomial Ridge captures broad structural trends (R² = 0.608), while tree ensembles effectively capture non-linear ecological interactions across features, delivering high predictive accuracy with tight residual bounds.

Prediction bands use empirical 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of validation residuals ([-3.73, +3.98] pp/yr), providing realistic confidence bounds around each site's predicted coral trajectory.

**4\. Factor Analysis**

Current-observation variables are compared against the next observed coral change using Spearman rank correlation, applied consistently to all 22 production features and two NOAA context variables so they can be viewed on one common scale. Narrative flags (anchor, trash, bleaching mentions) are additionally presented as differences in mean next change between mentioned and not-mentioned groups. These are descriptive, unadjusted lagged associations, not causal effects: repeated islands, irregular survey intervals, multiple comparisons, regional heat proxies, mean reversion and reporting intensity all limit interpretation. Correlation is used here only to flag whether a proposed factor has a measured relationship worth a field-verification question; it is never converted into a percentage of reef loss.

**5\. Assumption Boundaries**

* An island label is assumed sufficiently comparable across survey years; site-composition changes remain possible and large movements are verified against source reports.

  * Annualised change summarises the interval between two surveys; events between them are unobserved.

  * Earlier patterns are assumed to carry limited information about later years; forward validation tests this assumption rather than guaranteeing it.

  * Fold-local median imputation is acceptable for model comparison, but missingness may be systematic and is retained (not hidden) in the processed data.

  * The 56-island coordinate table's original retrieval script is not retained, so coordinates must be independently verified before any regulatory use.

  * The top quartile of predicted decline is a field-work queue, not an ecological carrying-capacity threshold.

**6\. Reef-Adjacent Economic Estimate**

&nbsp;

Two supplementary economic estimates were calculated alongside the priority queue: a reef-adjacent economy estimate and a season-rest comparison. Both are descriptive arithmetic on published, Malaysia-specific visitor and spending figures, not outputs of the predictive model, and both are excluded from the scored Gradient Boosting model described in Section 3\.

&nbsp;

The reef-adjacent economy estimate multiplies each park's annual visitors by the national average spending per domestic visitor, RM410.23, from DOSM's Domestic Tourism Survey 2024, and a 10% coefficient for the share of that spending attributable to reefs, from Spalding et al. (2017). Peninsular and Labuan parks use their 2013-2017 average from the Department of Marine Park Malaysia's published series; Sabah parks use 2024 totals from Sabah Parks. Summed across the ten parks with a published visitor count, this yields RM60.09 million a year, covering 30 of the 40 ranked monitoring units. The remaining ten units, including Malacca and several Sabah dive sites, have no published park-level visitor count and are excluded rather than estimated.

&nbsp;

The season-rest comparison applies the same method to the four parks that contain at least one high-priority unit, nine of the ten. It compares one month of foregone park spending, RM23.72 million, against the reef-adjacent value those parks would generate over a 10 to 15 year coral recovery period, RM284.66 million to RM426.99 million, using the recovery window reported by James Cook University (2019). Because both figures are derived from the same base spending and the same two coefficients, the ratio between them follows directly from those assumptions rather than from an independent measurement, and this is stated explicitly rather than presented as a finding.

&nbsp;

Both estimates document their own assumptions and limitations, including the age of the Peninsular visitor series (2017), reliance on a single global coefficient rather than one estimated for Malaysia, and the simplification of treating an entire park's visitor base as attributable to a single flagged unit. Earlier figures without a verifiable source, including an RM842.5 million "assets at risk" estimate and a room-count-based accommodation projection, were identified during review and removed.

**FINDINGS**

**4.1 Observed Trends and the Tourism Data Gap**

![][image5]

*Figure 2\. Unbalanced annual means with surveyed-unit counts and the paired 2024–2025 comparison.*

The same 39 monitoring units surveyed in both 2024 and 2025 averaged 44.98% live coral cover in 2024 and 40.22% in 2025 — a paired decline of 4.76 percentage points. This paired comparison, which tracks the same units across both years, is preferred over subtracting two changing annual samples of different composition.

![][image6]

*Figure 3\. Verified 2000–2017 visitor context and the unresolved island-level exposure gap.*

The verified marine-park visitor series covers only 2000–2017 aggregates. No recent, verified island-level visitor-exposure series is available, so the available totals cannot identify how many visitors, vessels, anchor drops, or wastewater loads reached any single monitoring unit. ReefSafe therefore does not, and cannot, estimate tourism's causal contribution to coral change from current data.

&nbsp;

&nbsp;

![][image7]

*Figure 5\. Observed coral change against selected Gradient Boosting model predictions.*

The model demonstrates strong, consistent predictive stability across all evaluated survey years, maintaining R² between 0.81 and 0.95 and low error (MAE ~1.38–2.14 pp/yr). The actual versus predicted scatter plot (Figure 5) confirms that predictions closely align with observed coral-cover trajectories across both typical survey cycles and acute bleaching event years. The displayed bounds use empirical 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of validation residuals ([-3.73, +3.98] pp/yr), providing high confidence for proactive site management.

**4.3 Associated Factors**

![][image8]

*Figure 6\. Lagged descriptive relationships for regional heat and report-mention indicators.*

The strongest negative all-factor association is coral cover relative to the regional average (Spearman ρ \= \-0.320, n \= 346, p \< 0.001), followed by current coral cover (ρ \= \-0.295) and current change rate (ρ \= \-0.218). These are condition signals — islands further above their regional baseline tend to fall back towards it — not identified causes, and may partly reflect mean reversion. Regional maximum DHW has a weak negative association with next observed change (ρ \= \-0.10, p \= 0.051, n \= 348): this supports a field-verification question, not a causal claim, since station-level heat is a regional proxy and repeated observations are not independent.

![][image9]

*Figure 7\. NOAA regional thermal context, explicitly excluded from the scored model.*

Most measured factors have weak or very weak individual associations with next observed change. Units whose reports mention anchor damage or bleaching show a smaller subsequent decline than units without those mentions (−0.43 vs −1.18 and −0.48 vs −1.35 pp/yr), while trash mentions coincide with a slightly larger decline (−1.05 vs −0.66 pp/yr). None of these differences is statistically significant (p \> 0.5); the pattern likely reflects reporting intensity and site-specific circumstances as much as impact severity, and is presented descriptively rather than as a ranked cause list.&nbsp;

**4.5 Economic Context**

The Department of Marine Park Malaysia booklet Total Economic Value of Marine Biodiversity: Malaysia Marine Parks reports a rounded annual Total Economic Value of RM8.7 billion from studies conducted during 2011–2015 for six evaluated archipelagos: Pulau Payar, Pulau Perhentian, Pulau Redang, Pulau Tioman, Pulau Tinggi, and Pulau Labuan.

![][image10]

*Figure 8\. Source-transcribed DMPM component values (calculated sum RM8.68699 billion before headline rounding).*

This benchmark is historical context. It is not a current national reef total, a ReefSafe revenue estimate, an island-level allocation, an avoided-loss figure, or a net present value, and ReefSafe does not recalculate it to current prices or apportion it across individual islands.

## **4.6 Reef-Adjacent Economy and Season-Rest Context**

Two supplementary metrics estimate tourism spending tied to reefs using published data rather than model predictions.

### **1\. Reef-Adjacent Economy: RM60.09M / year**

This represents the estimated tourist spending attributable to reefs across 10 marine parks with published visitor data.

* **Formula:** Annual Visitors × RM410.23 (average spend per visitor) × 10% (reef-attribution share).  
* **Context:** This is a minimum baseline. Ten other monitoring units lack published visitor counts and are excluded.

| Terengganu Marine Parks | 275,295 | RM112.93M | RM11.29M |
| Mersing Marine Parks | 208,734 | RM85.63M | RM8.56M |
| Tioman Marine Parks | 208,695 | RM85.61M | RM8.56M |
| Pulau Payar Marine Park | 122,124 | RM50.10M | RM5.01M |
| Tun Sakaran Marine Park | 100,369 | RM41.17M | RM4.12M |
| Sipadan Island Park | 36,719 | RM15.06M | RM1.51M |

| **Total** | **1,464,770** | **RM600.89M** | **RM60.09M** |

### **2\. Season Rest vs. Long-Term Revenue**

Four parks (Terengganu, Mersing, Tioman, and Labuan) house 9 of the 10 high-priority units and generate a combined RM284.66M in visitor spending annually, of which RM28.47M (10%) is reef-adjacent.&nbsp;

* **1 Month of Rest (Closure):** −RM23.72M (one-twelfth of annual visitor spending).&nbsp;  
* **10–15 Year Recovery Period:** \+RM284.66M to RM426.99M in reef-adjacent revenue (RM28.47M × 10–15 years).&nbsp;  
* **Context:** This 12× to 18× ratio is a mathematical comparison based on published inputs, not an empirical forecast of whether resting actually improves coral health.

### **Limitations & Assumptions**

* **Data gaps:** The Department of Marine Park series ends in 2017\. Pahang’s 2017 drop in visitors may reflect an incomplete year rather than a true decline.  
* **Conservative estimates:** The RM410.23 spend average includes day trips. Because overnight and foreign tourists typically spend more, these totals are a floor.  
* **Global coefficients:** The 10% reef-attribution share is a global average, not specific to Malaysia.  
* **Generalization:** Full park visitor counts are used as proxies for individual high-priority units within them (e.g., all of Tioman's visitors are counted for the Seri Buat unit).

**OUTPUT (DASHBOARD)**

ReefSafe's findings are delivered through an interactive dashboard designed for a reef manager to use without any statistical background. The workbook has four linked sheets:

* Dashboard — the decision screen. A single yellow input cell lets the user select any monitored island; the sheet then updates to show that island's current live coral cover, its most recently observed change, the model's predicted next change, its prediction confidence interval, its conservation priority tier, the recorded stressor evidence (e.g. NOAA thermal stress observed, anchor or trash mentions), and an evidence-matched priority action such as “Coordinate targeted bleaching survey” or “Check mooring buoys and anchoring controls.”

  * Priority\_Data — the full ranked table of all 40 currently scored units, supporting the Dashboard's dropdown and allowing a programme lead to work down the queue past the top ten shown in this report.

  * History\_Data — the underlying 404-row monitoring-unit/year panel (2012–2025) that every prediction and chart in this report and dashboard is drawn from, so any figure can be traced back to its source rows.

  * Model\_Check — the multi-year validation diagnostics (per-year MAE, RMSE, R² and bias) reproduced from Section 4.2 of this report, ensuring full transparent accountability for model performance.

The dashboard displays high-confidence prediction intervals and priority action recommendations so that conservation leaders can proactively allocate resources to the most vulnerable reef ecosystems. The workbook requires no add-ins and opens in any current version of Excel or a compatible spreadsheet application.

**CONCLUSION**

ReefSafe delivers high-precision predictive intelligence for proactive reef conservation and sustainable marine tourism. By combining nineteen years of Reef Check surveys, regional NOAA thermal data, coordinate and grouping references, and published economic context into one reproducible pipeline, the platform accurately forecasts live coral cover trajectories across Malaysia's marine parks. The selected Gradient Boosting architecture achieves an outstanding 69.9% improvement in MAE over the naive baseline (1.79 vs 5.93 pp/year) with R² = 0.914, providing reliable site-level predictions that empower authorities to schedule targeted ranger inspections and deploy timely conservation interventions before irreversible coral loss occurs.

The queue merges nineteen years of Reef Check surveys, coordinate and grouping data, and published economic context into one reproducible pipeline that names, for each high-priority island, the specific evidence a ranger should check next.

At the same time, ReefSafe maintains clear scientific boundaries regarding unmeasured variables. It does not estimate arbitrary carrying-capacity quotas, does not calculate tourism's causal share of reef change in the absence of island-level visitor-tracking data, does not convert DMPM's 2011–2015 historical valuation into current commercial revenue or an unverified per-island figure, and does not treat predictions as guarantees of specific intervention outcomes. Where the project does provide current ringgit figures on reef-adjacent tourism—such as the RM60.09M/year reef-adjacent economy and season-rest comparisons—these figures are presented as rigorous descriptive arithmetic on published visitor and spending data, kept outside the scored predictive model, and governed by a transparent assumption register.

**Real-World Impact and Implementation Pathway**

ReefSafe is designed to slot into work state marine park agencies already do, rather than to require a new institution. The natural adopter is the Department of Marine Park Malaysia (DMPM) and state-level marine park and fisheries offices, working from the same Reef Check Malaysia survey cycle this project already consumes. Rollout follows a phased timeline: each phase has a clear owner and only begins once the previous phase's result is known, rather than proceeding on a fixed calendar alone.

## **Implementation Timeline**

| Phase | Timeframe | What happens | Owner |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Phase 0 – Setup | Immediate – first quarter of adoption | Deliver the dashboard to DMPM and the piloting state office; refresh the model on the latest Reef Check release; confirm Seri Buat's priority ranking and flagged issue (mooring/anchoring damage) still hold. | Data analyst |
| Phase 1 – Field verification | Following quarter | Reef scientist reviews confidence labels and evidence for the top-ranked units; field ranger team conducts an on-site inspection at Seri Buat to confirm the flagged issue is real and active. | Reef scientist / Field ranger team |
| Phase 2 – Pilot decision and rest month | Same quarter, timed to a low-tourist period | DMPM or the state fisheries office reviews the verification report and approves (or declines) a one-month rest period at Seri Buat, paired with a redirected homestay, wellness or culinary package for affected local operators. | DMPM / state fisheries office |
| Phase 3 – Recording results | Immediately after the pilot, and again at the next annual survey | Log local income data from the pilot month; log the next observed coral-cover change at the following survey cycle. Report both to MOTAC/DMPM before deciding whether to extend the approach. | Programme lead |
| Phase 4 – State-level scale | Once Seri Buat's results are reviewed | If income results are non-negative, extend the rest-and-pivot model to the remaining Johor cluster (Mertang, Mensirip, Tinggi, Lima, Sibu); begin NOAA data-eligibility request; start a voluntary visitor-data-sharing pilot with willing operators. | Programme lead / DMPM |
| Phase 5 – National scale | Once the Johor cluster results are reviewed | Extend to Reef Check Malaysia's full island list; admit NOAA and verified visitor data into the scored model if eligibility and tracking are confirmed; explore regional expansion to other Coral Triangle countries. | DMPM / MOTAC |

*Each phase's start is conditional on the previous phase's result being reviewed, not on a fixed date — this keeps the pathway realistic if any single step takes longer than expected.*

**Actionable insights**

Government data shows that a reef's real economic value comes mostly from people enjoying its beauty (RM8 billion a year), not from ticket sales or entry fees (RM4.6 million a year). This means protecting reef health protects far more value than tourism income alone. It also supports a direction Visit Malaysia 2026 (VM2026) has already stated — a shift toward quality over quantity in tourism growth, and a stated aim to promote lesser-known destinations to ease overtourism at popular sites. Each table below splits recommendations into short-term (usable now, with current data and existing programmes) and long-term (dependent on data or infrastructure that does not yet exist), so the horizon of each action matches the evidence that actually supports it.

## **1\. What Travel Agencies and Operators Can Do**

| Horizon | Action |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Short-term** | Register site-specific fixes — a mooring buoy at Mertang/Tinggi/Seri Buat, a waste audit at Mensirip/Tenggol — as Tourism Project applications under MOTAC's existing MyTQA licensing scheme, making them eligible for current government funds and incentives without a new programme. |
| **Short-term** | Pursue Eco-Host Malaysia certification (an existing MOTAC course) and use it as the credential behind eco-tourism marketing built on ReefSafe's own recorded evidence (e.g. “no anchor damage recorded, mooring buoys installed \[date\]”). |
| **Short-term** | Sell eco-tourism packages where a small, disclosed fee funds the one specific fix named in the priority queue for that site. |
| **Short-term** | Operators across the five Johor sites (Mertang, Mensirip, Tinggi, Lima, Sibu) pool resources into one shared regional fix — mooring buoys/anchoring inspection at four sites and a waste audit at the fifth — rather than each operator applying separately. |
| **Long-term** | Share boat-trip and visitor records as a condition of continued licensing/incentive eligibility, closing the island-level tourism-exposure gap the report identifies as its central limitation. |
| **Long-term** | Once several seasons of shared data exist, support a proper test of tourism's share of reef change at specific sites — something no current Malaysian dataset can do. |

## **Where to Focus First: the Johor Cluster**

Five of the report's ten highest-priority sites sit in a single state — Johor — which is why these are shown together rather than folded into the general action tables above. This concentration is what makes a shared regional programme, rather than five separate one-off fixes, the more sensible response.

| Site | State | What was found | Fix needed |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Mertang | Johor | Mooring/anchoring damage | Mooring buoys, anchoring inspection |
| Mensirip | Johor | Waste/wastewater | Waste audit |
| Tinggi | Johor | Mooring/anchoring damage | Mooring buoys, anchoring inspection |
| Lima | Johor | Mooring/anchoring damage | Mooring buoys, anchoring inspection |
| Sibu | Johor | Mooring/anchoring damage | Mooring buoys, anchoring inspection |

*Note: there is currently no reliable data to say which state has “too much” tourist infrastructure — that claim would need information the project does not have. The pattern shown here is where the recorded evidence currently concentrates, not a judgement about Johor's tourism levels.*

## **2\. What Local Communities Can Do During Off-Season Rest**

Resting the four highest-priority parks (Terengganu, Mersing, Tioman, Labuan) for one month costs an estimated RM23.72 million in lost spending. Rather than treating this as pure loss, redirect it through programmes government is already funding in 2026–2027.

| Horizon | Action |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Short-term** | Route boardwalks, viewing platforms and rest-period exhibits through MOTAC's Homestay Experience Programme (829,803 participants and RM54.9 million generated for local communities in 2024), rather than building standalone infrastructure. |
| **Short-term** | Pitch a reef-conservation excursion (forest walk, spa, traditional massage) for inclusion in Tourism Malaysia's current roster of 36 wellness packages, open until 31 December 2026\. |
| **Short-term** | Package a rest-month “reef conservation \+ local food trail” experience under VM2026's own named niche segments (nature-based, experiential, wellness, gastronomy tourism). |
| **Short-term** | Apply Budget 2026/2027's personal tax relief for local attractions/cultural programmes, and the tax exemption on increased tour-package income, to give domestic visitors and operators a direct financial reason to take part during the rest month. |
| **Long-term** | Run the pilot rest month at Seri Buat and log income recovery in the same History\_Data panel used for coral tracking, producing a real answer — not an assumption — on whether income recovers. |
| **Long-term** | Only scale the rest-and-pivot model to the full Johor cluster once the Seri Buat pilot shows a measurable, repeatable result. |

## **3\. What Government Can Do**

| Horizon | Action |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Short-term** | Coordinate a single Johor state-level mooring/waste programme covering Mertang, Tinggi, Lima and Sibu (mooring buoys and anchoring inspection) and Mensirip (waste audit) together, rather than funding five separate site fixes — since 5 of the report's 10 highest-priority sites sit in this one state. |
| **Short-term** | Fund flagged-site fixes through the existing Budget 2026/2027 tourism allocation, rather than creating a new conservation budget line. |
| **Short-term** | Give ReefSafe's “stable and quiet” site shortlist to state campaigns (Visit Johor, Visit Terengganu, Visit Sabah) as evidence-based content for the quality-over-quantity direction VM2026 has already announced. |
| **Short-term** | Direct the Department of Environment (DOE) to prioritise a discharge-compliance audit — checking for valid permits and untreated effluent under the Environmental Quality Act 1974 — at Mensirip and Tenggol, the two sites ReefSafe's own priority queue already flags for waste/wastewater. This gives the queue's own “Inspect waste/wastewater” recommendation a named enforcing agency and existing legal basis. |
| **Short-term** | Cross-check whether Mensirip and Tenggol already sit within DOE's National Marine Water Quality Monitoring Programme (95 island stations). If yes, request that water-quality data as a free, verified input to strengthen the evidence behind the flag; if no, prioritise adding a station there, since marine park islands are already a named category in that programme. |
| **Short-term** | Publish dashboard results with the same transparency MOTAC already applies to Homestay Programme statistics, to build early public trust. |
| **Long-term** | Confirm NOAA thermal-data eligibility in writing so regional heat context can be admitted into the scored model. |
| **Long-term** | Fund small-scale package sewage treatment plant upgrades or septic system replacement for resort operators on flagged islands (Mensirip, Tenggol), since these islands are unlikely to be reachable by Indah Water Konsortium's connected sewer network, which mainly serves urban Peninsular Malaysia. Track progress against Malaysia's national target of halving untreated wastewater by 2030\. |
| **Long-term** | Build a public, tier-only version of the dashboard into Tourism Malaysia's Mastercard-built Travel Malaysia app, to support differentiated entry pricing or loyalty incentives once that infrastructure matures. |
| **Long-term** | Use existing visa-free and sales-mission channels (e.g. to China, India) to market quiet-site and homestay packages to fast-growing source markets, aligned with the National Tourism Policy (2020–2030). |

## **4\. What NGOs Can Do**

| Horizon | Action |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Short-term** | Partner with the Homestay Experience Programme and Eco-Host Malaysia network to help collect the missing boat-trip and visitor data at the community level. |
| **Short-term** | Use the “beauty is worth more than tourism income” finding to support Budget 2026/2027 incentive applications, since it does not depend on proving visitor growth. |
| **Long-term** | Help verify island coordinate data and build a trustworthy accommodation record for flagged sites, feeding into MOTAC's Tourist Accommodation Premises registration system. |
| **Long-term** | Support multi-year, community-based monitoring that could eventually supply the verified island-level visitor data the model currently lacks. |
| **Long-term** | Support community-level water-quality monitoring near flagged waste/wastewater sites, complementing DOE's existing island monitoring stations rather than duplicating them. |

*Caveat: none of the government or MOTAC programmes referenced above currently use ecological monitoring data as an eligibility input, and Indah Water Konsortium's role on remote islands has not been independently confirmed — these are proposed integration points based on each institution's known mandate, not documented current practice. This framing preserves the evidence-bounded approach used throughout the rest of the report.*

**Commercial and Scalability Potential**

ReefSafe's realistic commercial path is as a decision-support layer rather than a standalone consumer product. Reef Check Malaysia and DMPM already produce the underlying survey data every year; ReefSafe adds measurable value on top of it without duplicating their monitoring effort. Two adoption models are plausible: (i) a licensed analytics module offered to state marine park authorities and NGOs on a subscription or grant-funded basis, priced per state or per archipelago rather than per user; and (ii) an open, publicly-visible predictive intelligence dashboard that lets dive operators, conservation NGOs and tourists themselves see which islands require targeted conservation action — turning transparency itself into a light-touch demand-side incentive for responsible site choice.

•        Near-term scalability: extending the same pipeline to Reef Check Malaysia's full island list as coordinate and coverage gaps close, and re-running it every survey season at near-zero marginal cost.

•        Medium-term scalability: admitting NOAA thermal variables into the scored model once DOSM eligibility is confirmed in writing, and adding verified island-level visitor or vessel-tracking data if it becomes available, which would let the model finally speak to tourism's share of reef change.

•        Regional scalability: the same reconciled-PDF-extraction-plus-gradient-boosting pattern applies directly to other Coral Triangle countries that run annual reef surveys but lack a unifying predictive intelligence layer.
